\title{Association schemes for diagonal groups}
\author{Peter J. Cameron\footnote{School of Mathematics and Statistics, North
Haugh, St Andrews, KY16 9SS, UK}\ \
and\
Sean Eberhard\footnote{London, UK}}
\date{}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
For any finite group $G$, and any positive integer $n$, we construct an
association scheme which admits the diagonal group $D_n(G)$ as a group of
automorphisms. The rank of the association scheme is the number of
partitions of $n$ into at most $|G|$ parts, so is $p(n)$ if $|G|\ge n$; its
parameters depend only on $n$ and $|G|$. For $n=2$, the association scheme is
trivial, while for $n=3$ its relations are the Latin square graph associated
with the Cayley table of $G$ and its complement.
A transitive permutation group $G$ is said to be \emph{AS-free} if there is
no non-trivial association scheme admitting $G$ as a group of automorphisms.
A consequence of our construction is that an AS-free group must be either
$2$-homogeneous or almost simple.
We construct another association scheme, finer than the above scheme if
$n>3$, from the Latin hypercube consisting of $n$-tuples of elements of $G$
with product the identity.
Keywords: association scheme, diagonal group, Latin square
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}
An \emph{association scheme} consists of a finite set $\Omega$
and a collection of non-empty binary relations $R_1,\ldots,R_r$ (where $r$ is
the \emph{rank} of the scheme) such that
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep0pt
\item the relations form a partition of $\Omega^2$;
\item one of the relations (say $R_1$) is equality;
\item all relations are symmetric;
\item given $i,j,k\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$, there is a non-negative integer
$p_{ij}^k$ such that, for all $(a,b)\in R_k$, there are exactly $p_{ij}^k$
points $c\in\Omega$ such that $(a,c)\in R_i$ and $(c,b)\in R_j$.
\end{enumerate}
In the literature, conditions (b) and (c) are sometimes relaxed. But it is
important for our application to keep these conditions. (See~\cite{cap} for
discussion of this point.)
Representing relations $R_i$ by matrices $A_i$, the conditions in the
definition can be expressed as follows:
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep0pt
\item $A_1+\cdots+A_r=J$, where $J$ is the all-$1$ matrix;
\item $A_1=I$, the identity matrix;
\item each matrix $A_i$ is symmetric;
\item for any $i,j,k$, we have $\displaystyle{A_iA_j=\sum_{k=1}^rp_{ij}^kA_k}$;
so the span of $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ over $\mathbb{R}$ is an algebra.
\end{enumerate}
See \cite{book} for more on association schemes.
\medskip
Let $G$ be a group and $n$ an integer at least $2$. The \emph{diagonal group}
$D_n(G)$ is a permutation group of degree $|G|^{n-1}$ generated by the
following elements:
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep0pt
\item the group $G^n$ acting by right multiplication on the right cosets of
the subgroup $H=\{(g,g,\ldots,g):g\in G\}$;
\item the automorphism group of $G$, acting simultaneously on each coordinate;
\item the symmetric group $S_n$, permuting the coordinates.
\end{enumerate}
It is well known that
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep0pt
\item $D_n(G)$ acts faithfully if and only if $G$ has trivial centre;
\item $D_n(G)$ is primitive if and only if $G$ is characteristically simple.
\end{enumerate}
In the case where $G$ is simple, these ``simple diagonal groups'' and their
primitive subgroups form one of the classes in the O'Nan--Scott theorem
\cite[Theorem 4.1A]{dm}.
The trivial association scheme has just two relations, equality and inequality;
its automorphism group is the symmetric group. More generally, we regard a
structure as being \emph{trivial} if it is invariant under the symmetric group.
In \cite{cap}, a permutation group $G$ on $\Omega$ is said to be
\emph{AS-free} if it is not contained in the automorphism group of a
non-trivial association scheme. This definition is similar in spirit to many
classical definitions in permutation group theory. For example, a group is
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item \emph{transitive} if there is no non-trivial $G$-invariant subset of
$\Omega$;
\item \emph{primitive} if it is transitive and there is no non-trivial
$G$-invariant partition of $\Omega$;
\item \emph{$2$-homogeneous} if there is no non-trivial $G$-invariant
undirected graph on $\Omega$.
\end{itemize}
It is shown in \cite{cap} that an AS-free group must be
$2$-homogeneous, or almost simple, or of diagonal type $D_n(G)$ with $n\ge4$
and $G$ simple. Our purpose here is to construct an association scheme
invariant under the diagonal group, and hence show that the last case cannot
occur.
\section{The pre-association scheme}
We begin by constructing a ``pre-association scheme'' on the set $G^n$ (a
structure satisfying conditions (a), (c) and (d) of the definition, but with
(b) replaced by ``$R_1$ is an equivalence relation on $\Omega$''). Then
factoring out the equivalence relation gives the required association scheme.
Our structure has one relation $R_\pi$ for each partition $\pi$ of the set
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, defined by the rule that for two $n$-tuples
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ and $b=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$,
\[a\mathrel{R_\pi}b\hbox{ if and only if }
(a_ib_i^{-1}=a_jb_j^{-1})\Leftrightarrow(i\equiv_\pi j),\]
where $i\equiv_\pi j$ means that $i$ and $j$ belong to the same part of $\pi$.
The matrices of these relations are symmetric and sum to the all-$1$ matrix.
We prove that their span over $\mathbb{R}$ is closed under multiplication.
Let $A_\pi$ be the matrix of the relation $R_\pi$, the $|G|^n\times|G|^n$
matrix whose $(a,b)$ entry is $1$ if $a\mathrel{R_\pi}b$, $0$ otherwise.
Let $B_\pi$ be the matrix of the relation $S_\pi$ defined by
\[a\mathrel{S_\pi}b\hbox{ if and only if }
(i\equiv_\pi j)\Rightarrow(a_ib_i^{-1}=a_jb_j^{-1}).\]
Thus we have
\[B_\pi=\sum_{\pi\preceq\sigma}A_\sigma,\]
where $\preceq$ is the order in the lattice of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$
ordered by refinement, with finer partitions below coarser ones. Now
M\"obius inversion in the lattice of set partitions (see
Stanley~\cite[Section 3.7]{ec1}) shows that the $A_\pi$
can be expressed as linear combinations of the $B_\sigma$. Thus the $A$ and
$B$ matrices have the same span, and it suffices to show that the span of
the $B$ matrices is closed under multiplication.
The $(a,b)$ entry of $B_\pi B_\sigma$ counts the number of $n$-tuples $c$
such that $a\mathrel{S_\pi}c$ and $c\mathrel{S_\sigma}b$. This means
that the ratios $a_ic_i^{-1}$ agree on parts of $\pi$, while the ratios
$c_ib_i^{-1}$ agree on parts of $\sigma$. This is zero unless the ratios
$a_ib_i^{-1}$ agree on parts of $\tau=\pi\wedge\sigma$. Assuming this does
hold, we choose elements $u_i$ and $v_i$ such that $u_i$ is constant on
parts of $\pi$ and $v_i$ constant on parts of $\sigma$, and such that
$u_iv_i=a_ib_i^{-1}$ for all $i$.
We claim that this can be done in $|G|^{|\pi\vee\sigma|}$ ways, where $|\rho|$
denotes the number of parts of $\rho$. For if we choose the value $u_i$, then
the value of $v_i$ is determined. Moreover, $u_i$ is constant on parts of $\pi$,
so $v_j$ is determined on these parts; and $v_j$ is constant on parts of
$\sigma$, so $u_j$ is determined on these. We see that the values are
determined on a part of $\pi\vee\sigma$ by the choice, and the results follow.
Now each choice as above gives a unique $c$ such that
\[a_ic_i^{-1}=u_i,\qquad c_ib_i^{-1}=v_i,\]
so the result is proved.
\bigskip
It is clear that these relations are invariant under right multiplication
by all elements of $G_n$, since $(a_ig_i)(b_ig_i)^{-1}=a_ib_i^{-1}$. They
are invariant under other transformations:
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep0pt
\item left multiplication by elements of $H$, since
\item automorphisms of $G$ acting coordinatewise.
\end{enumerate}
\section{Taking the quotient}
The orbits of $H$ acting by left multiplication as in (a)
above are precisely the right cosets of $H$ in $G^n$. Invariance of the
relations above shows that the quotient of the structure by this equivalence
relation has corresponding relations $\bar R_\pi$ induced on it. Now, if
$\pi$ is the relation of equality, then $R_\pi$ is precisely the relation of
lying in the same right coset of $H$, and so $\bar R_\pi$ is the relation
of equality. So, as well as the other relations defined above, we have
recovered the one missing axiom for association schemes.
Thus, we have constructed an association scheme on $H\backslash G^n$ (the
set of right cosets of $H$) invariant under right translation by $G^n$ and
automorphisms of $G$ acting coordinatewise.
To reach the full diagonal group we need to adjoin the symmetric group. This
clearly does not preserve the relations $\bar R_\pi$, but it induces ``weak
automorphisms'' of the association scheme; that is, it permutes these
relations among themselves. Taking the unions of orbits of $S_n$ on the
relations $\bar R_\pi$, we obtain an association scheme, whose relations are
indexed by the orbits of $S_n$ on set partitions of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$; that
is, simply the partitions of the integer $n$, expressions of $n$ as a sum
of positive integers with the summands in non-increasing order. See
\cite[Theorem 8.17]{book}.
The valency of the relation $R_\pi$ in the pre-association scheme is the
number of ordered $|\pi|$-tuples of distinct elements of $G$, and so is
non-zero if and only if $|G|\ge|\pi|$. In particular, all relations are
non-empty if and only if $|G|\ge n$. Passing to the quotient divides the
valency by $|G|$, and merging orbits under $S_n$ multiplies by the number of
set-partitions corresponding to a given partition of $n$. So, the rank is
equal to to the number of partitions of $n$ into at most $|G|$ parts, and is
equal to $p(n)$ if and only if $|G|\ge n$. (Thanks to Cheryl Praeger for this
observation.)
To summarise:
\begin{theorem}
There is an association scheme on $H\backslash G^n$ with rank equal to the
number of partitions of $n$ with at most $|G|$ parts, (so $p(n)$ if and only if
$|G|\ge n$), which is invariant under the diagonal group $D_n(G)$.
\end{theorem}
For example, when $n=3$, we obtain the Latin square graph of the Cayley table
of $G$ and its complement. The valency of the complement is
$(|G|-1)(|G|-2)$, so it is non-empty if and only if $n>2$.
\section{AS-free groups}
As noted above, a permutation group is \emph{AS-free} if it preserves no
non-trivial association scheme. A transitive permutation group is
\emph{primitive} if it preserves no non-trivial equivalence relation on its
domain; a primitive group is \emph{basic} if it preserves no Cartesian
structure on its domain~\cite{ps}. Moreover, a permutation group is
\emph{$2$-homogeneous} if it acts transitively on the set of $2$-element
subsets of its domain; and a group $G$ is \emph{almost simple} if
$T\le G\le\mathrm{Aut}(T)$ for some non-abelian finite simple group $T$.
\begin{theorem}
An AS-free permutation group is primitive and basic, and is either
$2$-homogeneous or almost simple.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
This is a combination of a theorem in \cite{cap} and the result of this
note. Specifically, if $G$ is imprimitive, then it preserves the
\emph{group-divisible} association scheme, whose relations are ``equal'',
``same part of the $G$-invariant partition'', and the rest. If $G$ is
primitive but not basic, it preserves a Hamming scheme (see~\cite{book}).
If $G$ is basic, then according to the O'Nan--Scott Theorem, it is affine
(that is, has an elementary abelian regular normal subgroup), or diagonal,
or almost simple. If $G$ is affine, then the matrices of the $G$-orbits on
pairs belong to the group algebra of the regular normal subgroup, and so
commute; adding each non-symmetric matrix to its transpose then gives an
association scheme, whose rank is the number of $G$-orbits on $2$-sets plus
one (for the diagonal), so is trivial if and only if $G$ is $2$-homogeneous.
If $G$ is contained in $D_n(T)$ for some non-abelian simple group $T$, then
$G$ preserves the symmetrised conjugacy class scheme of $T$. And finally, if
$G$ is contained in $D_n(T)$ for $n>2$, then $G$ preserves the association
scheme constructed above, which is trivial only in the case $n=2$. (We have
$|T|\ge60$, so relations corresponding to partitions with at most $60$ parts
are non-empty.)
\end{proof}
Note that any $2$-homogeneous group is AS-free. There exist AS-free almost
simple groups which are not $2$-homogeneous, but the situation is
not well understood. We record here some examples taken from \cite{cap}:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item $\mathrm{PSL}(3,3)$ and $\mathrm{PSL}(3,3).2$, degree 234 (numbers
$(234,1)$ and $(234,2)$ in the \textsf{GAP} list);
\item $J_2$, degree $1800$ (number $(1800,1)$).
\end{itemize}
\section{Further remarks}
\subsection{Latin squares}
A Latin square of order $n$ can be regarded as an orthogonal array of
strength~$2$ with $3$ factors. If $G$ is a group, we can describe this
orthogonal array very simply: it is the set of triples $(x,y,z)\in G^3$
with $xyz=1$. It is clear that this set is invariant under $G^3$ acting
as follows:
Moreover, the set also admits automorphisms of $G$ acting coordinatewise,
as well as permutations of the three coordinates with a small twist:
$xyz=1$ implies $yzx=1$ and $z^{-1}y^{-1}x^{-1}=1$, so odd permutations
must be combined with inversion. So this set of triples admits $D_3(G)$.
The corresponding Latin square, as an $n\times n$ array,
is obtained by indexing rows and columns by $G$ and writing $z$ in the
$(x,y)$ cell if $xyz=1$. The ``traditional'' Cayley table has $z$ in position
$(x,y)$ if $z=xy$. For the record, we match up these two representations with
ours.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item The orthogonal array definition has $xy$ entry $(xy)^{-1}$, so is obtained
from the traditional one by the permutation of letters which replaces each
letter by its inverse.
\item Represent the cosets of $H$ in $G^3$ by noting that each coset contains
a unique element of the form $(x,y,1)$; we regard this as indexing a cell
$(x,y)$ of a square array. Now the relation corresponding to the
partition $2+1$ of $3$ makes two of the three coordinate ratios equal. So
consider two coset representatives $(a_1,a_2,1)$ and $(b_1,b_2,1)$. If the
first and third coordinate ratios are equal then $a_1=b_1$; so this is the
relation ``same row''. Similarly, equality of the second and third rations is
the relation ``same column''. In the remaining case, $a_1b_1^{-1}=a_2b_2^{-1}$,
which is equivalent to $a_2^{-1}a_1=b_2^{-1}b_1$; so this is the relation
``same letter'' if we put entry $y^{-1}x$ in cell $(x,y)$. So this Latin square
is obtained from the orthogonal array form by the permutation of columns which
replaces each column label by its inverse.
\end{itemize}
We now extend this to higher dimensions. A group $G$ defines a Latin
hypercube $L$, the set of $n$-tuples $(g_1,\ldots,g_n)$ of group elements whose
product is the identity; these form an orthogonal array of strength $n-1$.
The set is invariant under cyclic permutations of the group elements, and
reversal together with inversion:
$(g_1,\ldots,g_n)\mapsto(g_n^{-1},\ldots,g_1^{-1})$.
Now we can define a map from $G^n$ to $L$ by the rule
This map is invariant under left multiplication by elements of $H$, so induces
a bijection $H\backslash G^n\to L$. Now the cyclic shift on $L$ is realised
by the cyclic shift on $H\backslash G^n$, while the reversal-and-inversion
of $L$ is induced by reversal on $H\backslash G^n$. Thus the
dihedral group is a group of weak automorphisms of the association scheme
on $H\backslash G^n$ with relations $R_\pi$, and fusing orbits gives an
association scheme. This association scheme does not admit the full diagonal
group, since only elements of the dihedral group act as coordinate permutations.
(In the case $n=3$, the diagonal group is equal to the full symmetric group.)
\subsection{Isomorphisms}
There exist superexponentially many strongly regular graphs with certain
parameters, for example Latin square graphs.
Our construction potentially gives many (though not superexponentially many)
non-isomorphic association schemes of
relatively large rank with the same parameters. As noted earlier, the parameters
depend only on $n$ and $|G|$, so we can choose an order for which many groups
exist. It is known that the number of groups of order $q=2^d$ is about
$q^{c(\log q)^2}$. However, we have not proved that non-isomorphic groups give
non-isomorphic association schemes.
